title: Eileen Gu defends Olympic gold in women’s freeski halfpipe
content:
LIVIGNO, Italy — The pressure was on Eileen Gu. When is it not?

The reigning Olympic champion has defended her freeski halfpipe title at the 2026 Milan Cortina Olympics, earning her third medal at these Winter Games and her sixth Olympic medal overall.

With this latest victory, Gu, who represents China, having switched her allegiance from the United States in 2019, further cements her legacy as the most decorated freestyle skier in history.

The 22-year-old had to fend off reigning world champion Zoe Atkin of Great Britain, who qualified in first place, and world No. 2 Li Fanghui of China. Fanghui won silver, and Atkin finished with bronze.

“Every day I was fighting. I gave my all every single day that I’ve been here, and that’s no joke,” Gu said after winning gold. “In all three events I showcased my best skiing and as far as performance goes, that’s all I can ask for — to be able to show the world the best that women’s skiing has to offer at the moment that it really counts.”

Adding to the tension, athletes had to wait a further 15 hours before taking the stage as the event was postponed from Saturday night to Sunday morning due to snowy conditions.

Gu’s gold-winning six-trick run impressed judges because of its amplitude and technical difficulty. It consisted of a right side 900, a left side 900 tail grab, switch 720 tail grab, and switch left side 720 Japan grab, followed by consecutive alley oops, one 540 mute grab and one 540 critical grab.

She pumped her fists down into the ground, knowing she had landed a near-perfect run. The fans cheered “Gu-Eileen, Gu-Eileen.”

Atkin landed a smooth and technically proficient first run, putting her in pole position with a score of 90.50.

Her amplitude — height above the pipe — impressed the judges as she soared 15 feet above the 22-foot wall of ice. Although she told the cameras she was nervous, her skiing didn’t show it.

“I believe we’ve seen the highest level for women’s halfpipe event ever today,” said Joe Schuster, Atkin’s coach.

But Gu, who lost her balance on the first run, responded on her second with a score of 94.50. Atkin knew she had to reply, but fell trying to perform an alley-oop trick on her second run. It was that trick that had previously caused Atkin a “mental block” which she has since overcome.

It all came down to the last run. Gu was in first position, leading by 2.5 points. She bettered her second run by 0.75 of a point, piling the pressure on Atkin. Going eighth, she had to wait for four more athletes to compete, including world No. 1 Atkin, before learning her fate.

“The reason I love the records so much is that it’s not about man or woman. I’m the most decorated freeskier of all time, male or female,” Gu said. “I have the most gold medals ever, male or female. That’s a testament to competitive strength, it’s mental strength. It’s being able to perform under pressure, it has nothing to (do with) if you’re a boy or a girl.

“Being able to lead the way and pioneer the sport is something I never imagined I’d be able to do but I’m really honored and proud that I have.”

Svea Irving, a 23-year-old American ranked fourth in the world at the end of the 2025 season, was unable to complete a clean run in the finals. Having dealt with a knee injury in the months leading up to these Olympics, Irving fell on her first run of the finals, getting up gingerly. She missed her second run and, for a moment, appeared out of the competition. Irving returned to give it a go for a third run, but bailed out after three tricks and didn’t finish. She ended the day 11th of the 11 skiers to enter the pipe.

Irving, from Winter Park, Colo., reached Milan Cortina alongside her brother, Birk Irving, who also reached the finals in freeski halfpipe.

Kate Gray, the other American to reach Sunday’s women’s final, went down on each of her first two runs before completing a clean third attempt and finishing with her arms raised at the bottom of the pipe. Only 19, the Mammoth Lakes, Calif., native posted a 66.50 score and finished 10th overall.

As she stepped onto the podium, Gu, wearing a gold ribbon in her hair, raised one fist in the air before she sang China’s national anthem.

It has been a particularly intense programme for Gu, all by her own doing. After qualifying on Thursday, Gu said she was “exhausted.” She is the only female freestyle skier competing in all three freeski events — slopestyle, halfpipe and big air — at the Winter Games, but halfpipe is her preferred event and the one she really wanted.

At the start of the Winter Olympics, it was not in Gu’s plan to compete in the big air. So much so that after she secured silver in the slopestyle two weeks ago, her mother Yan Gu called a team meeting and said, “Let’s move on to halfpipe.”

However, Gu felt confident in her jumps. “If I can compete, why not?” she said. The problem was Monday’s big air final clashed with one of the three training sessions leading up to Thursday’s qualification, forcing Gu to miss it.

The Stanford student criticized the scheduling of her freeski events, saying the program “doesn’t make sense” and is “really unfair.”

“The fact I made big air finals should not disadvantage me for being the only woman trying to compete in three events,” she said.

In a statement to The Athletic, FIS communications director Bruno Sassi said, “Constructing the Olympic competition program is a complex process.”

Instead, Gu just had to “hustle” to make up for the missed training.

Her two silvers and one gold match her three-medal haul at the 2022 Beijing Winter Olympics — two golds and one silver — the only difference being she did not retain her big air title.

There is a saying in Chinese to “lie flat,” said Gu on Thursday. Now she can “lie flat” knowing her work in Italy is done.

— The Athletic‘s Brendan Quinn contributed to this report.
